title: The Best Tech Products Will Overcome Volatile Times
text:

https://www.barrons.com/articles/what-the-iphones-success-tells-us-about-the-next-big-product-cycle-51549064551 The Best Tech Products Will Overcome Volatile Times By Feb. 1, 2019 6:42 p.m. ET Order Reprints Photograph by Adrian Bretscher/Getty Images for Kaspersky Lab Text size
Excuses, excuses. Companies love to point to external factors when they underperform, often ignoring issues with their own product line.
Already this year, Apple (ticker: AAPL), Intel (INTC), and Nvidia (NVDA) have blamed China’s deteriorating economy as a major driver for their subpar numbers. But even as macro conditions have dominated the technology narrative in recent months, investors should keep an open mind: History is littered with examples of good products succeeding in turbulent times. Often, the micro trumps the macro.
The addressable markets for technology remain massive, so great products offering significant performance increases, often at lower cost, win even in lackluster economies. And this can translate into meaningful returns for investors, no matter the macro environment.
Consider the groundbreaking iPhone. It came out in June 2007, but didn’t really take off until a year later, when the company added a 3G connection and opened the App Store. That was July 2008, just as the economy was slipping into its darkest days since the Great Depression. In the five years following the iPhone’s debut, Apple’s stock nearly quintupled. The S&P 500 fell 9%.
Likewise, Nvidia launched a lineup of graphics cards based on its Pascal architecture in May 2016, in the middle of a semiconductor sector downturn. Nvidia’s new chips offered a massive 50% to 100% leap in gaming performance over the prior generation. They drove a large upgrade cycle and spurred a string of positive earnings surprises. Over the following two years, Nvidia’s stock price rose 443%, versus the S&P 500’s 30% return.
So what’s the next product-led tech story that could overcome brewing macro worries? One strong contender is Advanced Micro Devices (AMD), the chip maker that makes processors that are the main computing brains for PCs, servers, and graphics cards.
Late last year this column suggested that AMD could be a big winner in 2019, due to its opportunity to gain share against Intel in the lucrative server chip market. AMD stock has risen 23% since then, while Intel shares are up just 2%.
But AMD could be just getting started on a multiyear product story. On Tuesday, the company gave solid sales-growth guidance for the full year and confirmed that its next-generation server chip, called Rome, will be launched in the middle of the year.
Later that evening, AMD CEO Lisa Su told Barron’s in a phone interview that she is extremely optimistic about the 2019 product pipeline, maintaining that demand driven by Rome’s big performance gains will help negate any effects from a slowing global economy.
“We get asked all of these questions about macro and what’s happening overall. I do agree those things are there, but in some sense you know it’s just a noisy environment,” she said. “For us, it is a product story. If you have a superior product, that will mitigate some of these macro impacts. That’s certainly our view.” Newsletter Sign-up
Industry analysts have said that AMD will have a chip technology manufacturing advantage for several years. Its Rome processor is based on seven-nanometer technology, while Intel’s next server chip will be on 10 nm and won’t ship until early 2020. Smaller nanometer manufacturing processes have historically allowed semiconductor companies to create faster, more power-efficient chips.
Senior Editor Ian Cutress at AnandTech, a widely-read technology website, told Barron’s that AMD’s consumer processor lineup this year could surpass Intel’s in performance. “Intel will not have a proper response to AMD’s mid-2019 products until 2020 at the earliest,” he wrote in an email.
Intel currently dominates the high-profit-margin data-center business, where it sells server chips to cloud computing providers and corporations. The segment generated sales of $23 billion for Intel in 2018, with operating profit of $11.5 billion. In comparison, AMD’s total 2018 sales were just $6.5 billion. Even taking a small portion of Intel’s server chip business would be a huge financial boon for AMD.
And the company is already making progress on that front. Last week, it confirmed that it had a mid-single-digit market share for server chips at the end of 2018, up from virtually nothing a year earlier. The company has predicted that it will hit 10% in the next four to six quarters.
CEO Su told Barron’s that Rome will offer two to four times the performance of its current-generation chip: “We believe we’ll set up a good share-gain story as we go through 2019—just given Rome’s competitiveness and the generational improvement that we’re seeing.”
Wall Street analysts are taking note of AMD’s potential. “The server chip market is a big, fast-growing market that is very profitable,” Stifel chip analyst Kevin Cassidy said in a phone interview on Thursday. “Rome is clearly going to be a faster design, and be more competitive against Intel...A global slowdown isn’t going to affect AMD,” due to its low market share.
He predicts that the company will capture 10% of the server chip market by the end of 2019. Cassidy added that AMD could “possibly” hit 20% by year-end 2020. Even that level remains below AMD’s all-time high of 25%, reached in 2006.
Cassidy has a Buy rating on AMD and a $34 price target on the stock, almost 39% above its $24.51 closing price on Friday.
The biggest sign that AMD is making progress in the server market came on Friday when Intel filed its annual report with the SEC. The industry giant added AMD to the data center competition section of its filing. May the best product win.
